description: One team member from Guadalajara, Mexico, tackling the Field Shift challenge. I’m building a simple web tool that uses NASA climate data (temperature and rainfall) to show how a changing climate affects crops in Jalisco and what farmers can do to adapt. My goal is to turn satellite data into clear, practical insights for local growers. Open to teammates with data analysis, data visualization or web development skills.
summary:
MaizeShift México is a decision-support tool that helps maize farmers explore crop rotations that protect soil and adapt to a changing climate. It uses NASA POWER data (1995–2025) for 38 agricultural regions across Mexico, plus any point the user clicks on the map, to show warming, rainfall variability, dry seasons, extreme-heat days and root-zone soil wetness. It adds NASA MODIS NDVI, GPM IMERG and SRTM terrain to look at vegetation cover, rainfall reliability and erosion risk.

The farmer enters soil type, irrigation and priorities (water, soil health, income, climate stability and input cost). The tool compares six rotations, including continuous maize as the current baseline. For each one it explains why it is suggested, the NASA evidence, expected benefits, information gaps and risks that need local review. Scenario sliders show how the ranking changes with less rainfall or more warming. A glossary and uncertainty notes explain the science in plain language, in English and Spanish.

MaizeShift supports, and does not replace, farmer judgment and local agronomic expertise.
details:
1. What does your project do and how does it work?

MaizeShift Jalisco is a free web-based decision-support tool that helps maize growers in Jalisco, Mexico, explore climate-smart crop rotations. The user picks a region on an interactive map, then chooses their soil type (sandy, loam or clay), irrigation level (rainfed or limited) and priorities (water security, soil health, income, stability under climate risk, low input cost).

For each region, the app fetches live NASA POWER data (1995-2025) for 2 m air temperature, bias-corrected precipitation, root-zone soil wetness and daily maximum temperature. It compares the recent period (2010-2025) with the earlier one (1995-2009) for the June-October growing season. It shows warming trends, rainfall variability, dry seasons, extremely hot days and soil wetness in interactive charts and a regional ranking.

The rotation explorer then estimates water supply (70% of season rainfall + usable soil water based on NASA root-zone wetness + irrigation) and heat pressure, and scores candidate rotations weighted by the farmer’s priorities. All data can be downloaded as CSV, and the interface is available in English and Spanish.

2. What benefits does it offer?

  • Turns complex NASA climate data into clear, visual and actionable information for non-experts.
  • Helps farmers and advisors compare rotations according to their own soil, water and economic priorities.
  • Shows how each region is changing (warming, rainfall, hot days, dry seasons), so decisions are based on evidence rather than intuition.
  • Free, bilingual, and needs no installation, only a browser.
  • Downloadable CSV data supports further analysis by researchers and technicians.

3. What impact does it aim to create?

We want to help maize growers in Jalisco adapt to a changing climate by making NASA Earth observation data accessible at the local level. Our goal is to support more resilient farming: better water use, healthier soils and reduced climate risk for smallholder farmers and the communities that depend on maize, a crop central to Mexico’s food security and culture. Because the tool is built on open NASA data and an open method, it can be extended to other crops and regions.

4. What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • NASA data: NASA POWER (AG community): T2M, PRECTOTCORR, GWETROOT, T2M_MAX.
  • Other data and services: Open-Meteo (current conditions in map popups, not NASA data) and Esri (satellite imagery and place names).
  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • Deployment: GitHub Pages.
  • Methods: least-squares trend analysis, period comparison, percentile-based dry-year estimates and a priority-weighted scoring model.
  • Hardware: none required, since it runs in any web browser.

5. What makes it creative and innovative?

  • It combines NASA climate data, soil wetness, soil type, crop characteristics and the farmer’s own priorities in one tool, instead of showing climate data alone.
  • It uses live NASA POWER data for each region’s coordinates, so nothing is pre-processed or hidden.
  • It lets farmers weight their priorities (water, soil, income, stability, cost), so the same data gives different results for different needs.
  • It is transparent: the method, assumptions and limitations are documented, and the data is downloadable.
  • It is bilingual and built for local use in Jalisco, not for a generic global audience.

6. What factors did the team consider?

  • Honesty about uncertainty: the tool gives climate signals, not yield forecasts, and is meant to be combined with local agronomic advice.
  • Data limitations: one grid point per region (cells of about 0.5° × 0.625°), model-based soil wetness, and no yield or irrigation data.
  • Simplified assumptions: crop and soil values are illustrative and should be replaced with local data and agronomist input.
  • Accessibility: free, bilingual, mobile-friendly and with no installation needed.
  • Transparency and reproducibility: documented method, clear thresholds (for example, a dry season is below 85% of the average) and CSV downloads.
  • Clear data sourcing: we label which data is from NASA and which is not.
  • Future work: integrate NASA SMAP soil moisture observations and MODIS/Landsat vegetation indices, and add local yield and farmer feedback.
